prompt: Why run several attention heads instead of one, at the same total width?

options.A: Heads run on different layers
options.B: Heads are spare copies for fault tolerance
options.C: Each head has its own softmax, so it can focus sharply on its own target (one on “river” for meaning, another on the previous word for grammar); one softmax would blur all needs into one average
options.D: More heads means more parameters

prompt: Why use three separate vectors (query, key, value) instead of the token's embedding for everything?

options.A: Embeddings can't be multiplied together
options.B: What a word looks for, what it matches on, and what it hands over are different jobs; separate learned matrices let each be tuned on its own
options.C: One vector is needed per attention head
options.D: To triple the model's memory for facts

prompt: How does “an LLM is a function, not a lookup table” explain hallucination?

options.A: The fact's token is missing from the vocabulary, so a similar token is substituted
options.B: It computes a plausible next token for any input from learned patterns; nothing checks that a source for the claim exists
options.C: It retrieves the nearest stored document and sometimes retrieves the wrong one
options.D: Hallucination comes only from sampling randomness; at temperature 0 it can't happen

prompt: Which backend operation has the same cost shape as attention over n tokens?

options.A: A hash lookup: constant time
options.B: A single sequential scan: n
options.C: A self-join comparing every row with every earlier row: about n²/2
options.D: A B-tree index lookup: log n

prompt: Why can one copy of a model's weights in GPU memory serve many users at once?

options.A: Each user gets a private copy of the weights
options.B: At inference the weights are only read, never written; each request's activations are separate and temporary
options.C: Users take turns, one request at a time
options.D: Weights are recomputed for every request

prompt: “bank” is used in water sentences and in money sentences. Where does its embedding row end up?

options.A: At random, because ambiguous words get no training signal
options.B: In the water cluster, because the first meaning seen wins
options.C: Two separate rows, one per meaning
options.D: Somewhere between the water and money clusters; attention picks the meaning later from context

prompt: Nobody labels “river” and “stream” as related. How do their embedding rows end up close?

options.A: Attention copies one row into the other at inference time
options.B: The tokenizer gives them neighbouring IDs
options.C: A dictionary of synonyms is loaded before training
options.D: They appear in similar sentences (“the ___ overflowed”), so training's corrections nudge their rows in similar directions

prompt: The score for “flooded” is bank's row · flooded's output row. After one training step, one column of bank's row moved a lot and another didn't move at all. Why?

options.A: Only the first column of each row is trainable
options.B: Columns are updated at random
options.C: Each column's nudge is proportional to the matching column of the other vector in the dot product; where that column is near zero, it barely affects the score, so its gradient is near zero
options.D: The column that didn't move had already reached its final value

prompt: A language needs 3× as many tokens for the same meaning. What follows? Pick all that apply.

options.A: Less text fits in the context window
options.B: Higher cost per request (billed per token)
options.C: The model has more weights for that language
options.D: Prefill gets faster

prompt: What does a gradient tell training?

options.A: How big a step to take (the learning rate)
options.B: Which neuron fired the most
options.C: For each number, how much the error would change if that number moved a little, so training can step each one the way that lowers the error
options.D: The correct next token at each position

prompt: A model writes a 100-token answer. Roughly how many times does the whole model run?

options.A: About 100 times: one pass per new token, each pass with the previous token appended
options.B: Once per sentence in the answer
options.C: Once per layer, so 32 times for a 32-layer model
options.D: Once: one pass produces the whole answer

prompt: The same paragraph costs more tokens in Hindi than in English. Why can't fine-tuning the model fix this?

options.A: The tokenizer is trained once, before the model, and then frozen; training the model never changes how text is split
options.B: Providers bill per word, not per token
options.C: Hindi needs more weights, and fine-tuning can't add weights
options.D: Fine-tuning could fix it, but it is too expensive to bother

prompt: Who decides a token's query, and how does it get good at finding useful words?

options.A: The tokenizer assigns a query to each token ID
options.B: A learned matrix W_Q multiplies the token's vector; training adjusts W_Q whenever a better query would have lowered the loss
options.C: It is drawn at random for each request
options.D: Engineers write rules for what each word should look for

prompt: Every token scores itself and every earlier token: n(n+1)/2 scores. How many scores for 4,000 tokens (per head, per layer)?
Why must the attention shares add up to 100%?

options.A: So that negative scores cancel out positive ones
options.B: So they can be read as probabilities of the next token
options.C: The next step is a weighted average; shares summing to 1 keep the blend on the same scale as the inputs, whatever the number of words
options.D: GPUs require normalized numbers

prompt: A model is 4,096 numbers wide and runs 32 attention heads. How many numbers wide is each head?
Remove all position information. What happens to “dog bites man” versus “man bites dog”?

options.A: The model crashes on repeated words
options.B: The tokenizer reorders the words alphabetically
options.C: Attention receives the same set of vectors either way, so it can't tell the two orders apart
options.D: Only the last word's meaning is lost

prompt: Compute the dot product of [2, 1, 0] and [1, 3, 5].
A tokenizer has no single piece for four spaces. What happens when you send it Python code indented with four spaces?

options.A: Nothing: whitespace is free
options.B: The spaces are dropped, so the code reaches the model broken
options.C: Each indent becomes several tokens, so the same code costs more and fills the context window sooner
options.D: The model refuses the input

prompt: Compare softmax([3, 1]) with softmax([2, 0]).

options.A: Identical: softmax depends only on the gaps between scores
options.B: The first gives the top score a bigger share, because its scores are larger
options.C: The first gives a flatter distribution
options.D: They can't be compared without knowing the vocabulary

prompt: Why does it help that similar words have nearby rows?

options.A: The model looks up the nearest training sentence
options.B: Nearby rows share storage, so the model is smaller
options.C: It lets the tokenizer merge synonyms into one token
options.D: Everything after the embedding is smooth math, so similar inputs give similar outputs: what was learned from “the river flooded” carries over to “the stream flooded”

prompt: Put one attention step for “bank” in the right order.

options.A: softmax of the values → dot with each key → add the query
options.B: query · each key → divide by √(head size) → softmax → weighted average of the values
options.C: weighted average of the keys, using the query as the shares
options.D: query · each value → softmax → weighted average of the keys

prompt: An embedding table has one row per vocabulary token. Vocabulary 100,000, width 4,096. How many learned numbers are in the table, in millions?
“The river bank flooded” and “The bank raised rates”. Compare the row looked up for “bank” in the two sentences.

options.A: Identical: the same ID reads the same row; context is mixed in later by attention
options.B: Different rows: the tokenizer picks the meaning from context
options.C: The same row, but the model edits it for the second sentence
options.D: Different rows, because their positions differ

prompt: Why do LLMs split text into subword pieces rather than single characters?

options.A: Characters can't represent languages other than English
options.B: Characters make sequences several times longer, and attention's work grows with the square of the length
options.C: A character vocabulary would be too large to store
options.D: A model can't learn spelling from characters

prompt: Why can't an LLM reliably count the r's in “strawberry”?

options.A: The word was rare in its training data
options.B: Softmax rounds small counts to zero
options.C: It receives a few opaque token IDs (like str + aw + berry); the letters inside each piece are not part of its input
options.D: Temperature adds randomness to counting

prompt: Context grows from 8,000 to 32,000 tokens. By what factor does the number of attention scores grow?
Which of these are learned weights (changed only by training), not per-request activations? Pick all that apply.

options.A: The query, key and value matrices (W_Q, W_K, W_V)
options.B: “bank”'s blended vector after attention in this sentence
options.C: The attention weights (softmax shares) for this sentence
options.D: The output table used to score the next token

prompt: Blend two values with a weighted average: 4 with share 75%, 8 with share 25%.
A model learns positions as a second table with one row per slot (slots 1 to 4,096). What does that design imply?

options.A: A hard length limit: there is no row for slot 4,097
options.B: Word order no longer matters
options.C: Positions keep updating during inference
options.D: The vocabulary must also have 4,096 tokens

prompt: In “The river bank flooded”, which words can “bank” attend to?

options.A: “The”, “river”, and “bank” itself
options.B: All four words
options.C: Only “flooded”
options.D: Only “river”

prompt: Softmax of the scores [2, 0]. What share does the first score get, in percent? (e ≈ 2.718)
Why can't a token ID be fed to the model as a plain number?

options.A: IDs are arbitrary labels: ID 500 is not “close to” 501 in meaning, so arithmetic on them is meaningless. Each ID selects a learned row (a vector) instead
options.B: IDs change from one request to the next
options.C: The model only accepts decimals between 0 and 1
options.D: IDs are too large for a GPU to handle

prompt: Why don't LLMs use whole words as tokens?

options.A: The vocabulary would need millions of entries and would still fail on any unseen word: a new name, a typo, a code identifier
options.B: Whole words make sequences too long
options.C: Whole words can't be turned into vectors
options.D: Attention can only compare pieces shorter than a word

prompt: How does byte-pair encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary?

options.A: Linguists write a list of prefixes and suffixes
options.B: Learn the pieces by gradient descent while the model trains
options.C: Start from single bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent neighbouring pair into a new token
options.D: Split at spaces and keep the most common words

prompt: Which of these tasks are hard for an LLM for the same reason as counting letters? Pick all that apply.

options.A: Reversing a word letter by letter
options.B: Finding words that rhyme
options.C: Translating a common sentence
options.D: Summarizing a paragraph
